title: Come, Ye Thankful People, Come
description: Henry Alford's harvest hymn to George Elvey's tune St. George, on Elvey's own harmony as Hymns Ancient and Modern printed it in 1861, for 2 to 4 singers: the first verse and the last, steady and bright, every line one breath.

credits.words: Henry Alford (1844; verse 4 as he revised it for The Year of Praise, 1867)
credits.tune: George J. Elvey, "St. George" (1861; today "St. George's, Windsor")
credits.arrangement: George J. Elvey's four parts (Hymns Ancient and Modern, 1861), adapted by Stackapella

licence.arrangement: Elvey's four parts as printed in Hymns Ancient and Modern (public domain: published 1861; the Index of Tunes names Elvey as composer and harmonizer; Elvey died 1893): his tune unchanged; one note to a syllable, so where the page's lower parts move on the bar's second beat under the tune's dotted note they move half a beat later with the next syllable (alto, tenor and bass at 48 to 49.5 and 52 to 53.5; the bass's printed A3 dotted minim and A3 crotchet sung as two crotchets, one for each of "God's own" (50, 51)), where the tenor's printed dotted minim and crotchet lie under two of the tune's minims its second note comes half a beat early with the second syllable (37, 45), and repeated notes printed as two minims come with the syllables (alto, tenor and bass at 20 and 21.5, tenor at 32 and 33.5); the alto revoiced to take the chord's third where the tune hasn't it, the tenor exchanging (alto: 16 and 17.5 G4, 20 and 21.5 F#4, 30 F#4 a third above the tune's low D4 at the cadence, 34 F#4, 36 B3, 42 B3, 43 D4, 44 E4, 46 G4, 48 G#4, 50 E4, 54 D4 so it and the bass don't move in octaves into line 8, 56 to 59 E4 E4 B3 B3, 60 to 62 D4 C4 B3, so the final chord has its third with 2 and 3 singers; tenor: 13 A3 for the tritone C4 to F#3, 20, 21.5, 29, 30 and 34 A3, 42 to 44 G3, 57 to 60 G3, 61 F#3, 62 D3, so the final chord has its fifth); the bass a fourth up instead of a fifth down into line 3's last note (22, G3) and an octave up at the start of line 6 (40, 41.5, G3), so neither line leaps twice; the bass holds its A3 at 29 instead of dropping the octave to A2, with the tenor on A3 and Elvey's passing G3 left out, so the chord is A and no seventh rises; breaths written in for beginners; beats are verse 1's, verse 4 the same 64 beats later
licence.source: Hymns Ancient and Modern for use in the services of the Church, with accompanying tunes, compiled and arranged under the musical editorship of William Henry Monk (London: Novello, 1861), Hymn 223, "Harvest", in G, printed in minims and written here in crotchets (4/4), kept in G; the tune is unnamed on the page and indexed as "St. George", "Dr. G. Elvey" composer and harmonizer, hymns 110 and 223 (Index of Tunes, p. xviii), and the preface (p. iv) thanks Elvey "for the use of the tune to Hymns 110 and 223"; the music, Elvey's four parts, and verse 1 as printed on the page after the music ("GOD" and "LORD" in small capitals written God and Lord), the Amen left out; read from the University of Toronto Faculty of Music Library's copy at archive.org/details/hymnsancientmode00unse (music page/n311, words page/n312, index page/n23, preface page/n9); verse 4 is Alford's own revised verse from The Year of Praise, edited by Henry Alford (London: Alexander Strahan, 1867), Hymn 275, headed "Elvey" (words at archive.org/details/yearpraisebeing00jonegoog, page/n381), in place of the verse Hymns Ancient and Modern prints, "glorious" sung in two syllables as the metre needs; the lower parts checked against the same hymn's music there, the same four parts in G (page/n380). Verses 1 and 4 because verse 4 answers verse 1 ("come" and "Harvest-home") and closes the hymn, while verses 2 and 3 tell the parable of the wheat and the tares. Breaths: each line's last note sung for one beat of its two, in every part, before beats 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 72, 80, 88, 96, 104, 112 and 120; the last note held its full two beats; the words dated 1844 in The Poetical Works of Henry Alford, fourth edition (London: Alexander Strahan, 1865), "After Harvest" (archive.org/details/poeticalworksofh00alfo), whose verse 4 is still the earlier "Then, thou Church triumphant, come"
